claim: A copy duplicates both the data buffer and the metadata, so changes made to the copy do not affect the original array.
quote: When a new array is created by duplicating the data buffer as well as the metadata, it is called a copy. Changes made to the copy do not reflect on the original array. Making a copy is slower and memory-consuming but sometimes necessary. A copy can be forced by using ndarray.copy.

claim: For a basic slice NumPy takes start, stop, step and length from PySlice_GetIndicesEx, advances the data pointer by stride times start, multiplies the axis stride by step, and sets the axis length to that number of steps; a non-positive length is turned into an empty axis.

locator: Indexing on ndarrays, section 'Basic slicing and indexing', first bullet on slice syntax
claim: For a positive-step basic slice, selected indices start at i and advance by k while remaining below j.
quote: This selects the m elements (in the corresponding dimension) with index values i, i + k, …, i + (m - 1) k where \(m = q + (r\neq0)\) and q and r are the quotient and remainder obtained by dividing j - i by k: j - i = q k + r, so that i + (m - 1) k < j.

claim: as_strided applies exactly the strides and shape it is given, so incorrect ones can make elements point to invalid memory and corrupt results or crash the program.
quote: as_strided creates a view into the array given the exact strides and shape. This means it manipulates the internal data structure of ndarray and, if done incorrectly, the array elements can point to invalid memory and can corrupt results or crash your program. It is advisable to always use the original x.strides when calculating new strides to avoid reliance on a contiguous memory layout.

claim: With order='C', reshape reads elements from the input and places them in the output in C index order, in which the last axis index changes fastest and the first axis index slowest.
quote: Read the elements of a using this index order, and place the elements into the reshaped array using this index order. ‘C’ means to read / write the elements using C-like index order, with the last axis index changing fastest, back to the first axis index changing slowest.

locator: numpy.reshape, parameter order, note after the 'F' description
claim: The 'C' and 'F' order options refer only to index order and take no account of the array's memory layout.
quote: Note that the ‘C’ and ‘F’ options take no account of the memory layout of the underlying array, and only refer to the order of indexing.

claim: NumPy attempts a no-copy reshape when the array is not contiguous in the requested order, and if that attempt succeeds it uses the computed strides instead of copying.
The no-copy attempt grows a run of new axes and a run of old axes until their extent products are equal, and only then checks whether those old axes can be combined.

locator: The N-dimensional array (ndarray), section 'Internal memory layout of an ndarray', opening paragraph
claim: The shape fixes the ranges of the indices, while a separate data-type object fixes how many bytes each item takes and how those bytes are interpreted.
quote: The ranges in which the indices can vary is specified by the shape of the array. How many bytes each item takes and how the bytes are interpreted is defined by the data-type object associated with the array.

locator: Array attributes, section 'Memory layout', table row ndarray.ndim
claim: ndim is the number of array dimensions, i.e. the array's rank.
quote: Number of array dimensions.

locator: Statistics: Reporting the Mean, Median and Standard Deviation / Coefficient of variation of Repeated Benchmarks
claim: Because a single benchmark result may be unrepresentative when timings are noisy, a benchmark can be run repeatedly.
quote: However benchmarks are often noisy and a single result may not be representative of the overall behavior. For this reason it’s possible to repeatedly rerun the benchmark.

claim: The median is the value that has half the data smaller and half the data larger.
quote: median - the median is the value of the point which has half the data smaller than that point and half the data larger than that point.

claim: MAD is the median of the absolute deviations of the observations from the data's median, and it is less affected by extremes in the tail than the average absolute deviation because tail values influence a median less than a mean.
quote:
- \( MAD = median (|Y_{i} - \tilde{Y}|) \)

where \(\tilde{Y}\) is the median of the data and |Y| is the absolute value of Y. This is a variation of the average absolute deviation that is even less affected by extremes in the tail because the data in the tails have less influence on the calculation of the median than they do on the mean.

claim: By default the whole work loop is timed; work inside the loop can be excluded from the measurement with pause/resume, but that is not recommended because it has high overhead.
quote: Normally, the entire duration of the work loop (for (auto _ : state) {}) is measured. But sometimes, it is necessary to do some work inside of that loop, every iteration, but without counting that time to the benchmark time. That is possible, although it is not recommended, since it has high overhead.

locator: Output Formats, JSON format, context object
claim: A benchmark report's context object records run metadata such as date, host, CPU, caches, load average, and library version, and extra custom context can be added to it.
quote: The context object contains information about the run in general, including the date, host, CPU, caches, load average, benchmark library version, and json_schema_version. Extra context added with benchmark::AddCustomContext or --benchmark_context is emitted as additional string fields in context.

claim: The benchmark program supplies the byte count to SetBytesProcessed itself, here iterations times the bytes per iteration.
quote:
state.SetBytesProcessed(int64_t(state.iterations()) *
                              int64_t(state.range(0)));

claim: Google Benchmark's documented hardware-counter feature requires a PMU and a build with counter support, currently using libpfm.
quote:
This feature is available if:

- The benchmark is run on an architecture featuring a Performance Monitoring Unit (PMU),

- The benchmark is compiled with support for collecting counters. Currently, this requires libpfm, which is built as a dependency via Bazel.

claim: A stepped slice selects i+n*k with 0 <= n < (j-i)/k, excluding the stop; positive steps stay below it and negative steps above it.
quote: The slice of s from i to j with step k is defined as the sequence of items with index x = i + n*k such that 0 <= n < (j-i)/k.

claim: PyTorch Linear applies an affine transformation with an additive bias, y = xA^T + b.
quote: Applies an affine linear transformation to the incoming data: y = xA^(T) + b.
